name: PCB Design

claims.claim_text: Board design is a learned skill acquired by doing rather than by study. Certification courses exist and are worth having, but they certify knowledge you already possess rather than teaching it, so the experience has to come first.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's more about getting certification of the knowledge you already have

claims.claim_text: There is no single correct board for a given circuit. Hand the same design to twenty designers and twenty different boards come back, which is why the craft is taught by experience rather than by rule.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you give the same design to 20 different designers, they'll give you 20 different layouts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Long-lived designs become unmaintainable through their tools. Working files end up in CAD packages that no longer exist, which turns a routine revision into a recreation exercise.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've seen stuff that's in some old CAD packages that don't even exist anymore
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: The generalist-versus-specialist question resolves differently by employer. One person is now expected to cover layout, sourcing, mechanical modelling and test, largely as a cost measure, but a designer who goes deliberately narrow will still find work.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's always going to be a niche job out there
claims.episode_title: CAD programs, Systems Design and Renewable Energy

claims.claim_text: That expectation does not extend upward. A large, expensive product will not be handed to a single person covering every discipline, and where it is, the compensation should reflect it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're not going to have just one person doing the whole thing
claims.episode_title: CAD programs, Systems Design and Renewable Energy

claims.claim_text: The scope of the role has widened beyond the board itself. A designer is now frequently expected to handle programming, the broader product design and even the surrounding web presence, because the available tools make it possible to ask.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not just the PCB anymore

claims.claim_text: Board work has an awkward duty cycle for an independent designer. Once files go out there is a gap that nothing fills unless the next project happens to start exactly then, whereas firmware work is continuous because there is always another improvement to make.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's just no, there's nothing carrying that gap

claims.claim_text: The open question that follows is one of scope: how large a combined hardware and firmware task a single fully utilised person can carry before a two-person team becomes more efficient. Adding a person costs coordination but buys specialisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: how big of a firmware and hardware task could one person take on

claims.claim_text: Speed and thoroughness are a project-level trade rather than a personal virtue. Some projects genuinely need good enough; others justify spending a week choosing the correct screw, and recognising which one you are on is the engineering judgment.
claims.quote_verbatim: the art of engineering is, is trading off

claims.claim_text: Where board revisions are expensive and faults are hard to track down, six months for a single revision can be the rational choice. The apparently absurd schedule follows from the cost structure rather than from slowness.
claims.quote_verbatim: six months to do a single rev of a board

claims.claim_text: Most of the work is front-loaded: on one experienced view, board design is ninety percent placement and setup, where setup means establishing the rules, clearances and outlines before any routing starts. Once the constraints are in place the routing is comparatively free.
claims.quote_verbatim: PCB design is 90% placement and set up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Checklists help but cannot be complete. Every board carries its own unique issues, and a checklist capturing every problem ever found would grow long enough that nobody would work through it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the checklist would be so long, it'd become unusable

claims.claim_text: What supplements the checklist is unstructured inspection: spending a full day panning around the finished board in different views, particularly the three-dimensional view, checking silkscreen, polarity marks and connector orientation. It catches the class of error no list anticipated.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll just spin that board around in 3D view for hours

claims.claim_text: A cheap habit worth building in: indicator LEDs on the power rail and on a spare digital output. They immediately expose conditions that are otherwise invisible, such as a part being powered parasitically through one of its I/O pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: One of the IOPins is powering the entire part

claims.claim_text: Part data is harder than it appears because one logical component is several physical ones. A 10K resistor in an 0603 size still has three different land patterns in the standards, so choosing the part does not finish the decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are three different sizes
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Two workflows follow and neither is correct. Either create every variant as its own part with its own number, or keep one or two and adjust on the board. Adjusting on the board suits a small company buying from distributors, while scale makes the formal approach unavoidable.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think the bigger you get, the more inevitable it is that you create a bigger monster

claims.claim_text: On-demand symbol and footprint services exist to absorb this work for a fee, but they do not resolve the underlying problem. Everything remains custom; it merely happens faster and someone else does it.
claims.quote_verbatim: nothing's solved. It's just, everything's custom and a little bit faster

claims.claim_text: Footprints shipped with a design tool are frequently unusable and tend to be oversized, which is why a working designer may end up building close to all of them by hand from the published standards mixed with personal convention.
claims.quote_verbatim: the footprints that come with Eagle are almost useless
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Even a borrowed footprint usually gets rebuilt, because the silkscreen outline is treated as part of the component rather than as decoration, and someone else's choices there rarely match.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I ever use someone else's footprint, I need to tear it apart and redo it anyway

claims.claim_text: The library burden drops sharply once the common passives and standard small-outline packages exist, but it never reaches zero. Every project turns up some obscure part needing a new footprint or at least a tweak to an existing one.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's some obscure chip I'm using that has some new footprint
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Reaching genuine proficiency in a professional board tool takes about a year of fairly intensive use. That number is what makes interface churn expensive: someone earning a living at this cannot absorb months of reduced effectiveness.
claims.quote_verbatim: it takes about a year, I would say, to become proficient at Altium

claims.claim_text: The argument that follows is for interface stability with an option to revert. Mechanical CAD is the comparison: its fundamental interaction model has barely changed in a very long time, and users remain effective across releases.
claims.quote_verbatim: keep the UI the same

claims.claim_text: One structural way a CAD vendor keeps contact with real use is an in-house hardware team designing real products on every daily build, so the tool is exercised by people whose actual output depends on it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we were forced to use each new daily build

claims.claim_text: Switching tools makes an expert temporarily slow and generates false defect reports, because a menu you cannot find feels exactly like a bug. Convention absorbed from one package gets mistaken for correctness.
claims.quote_verbatim: It must be a bug when it could just be, I don't know where that menu is
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: The separation worth keeping in mind is that an experienced designer learning a new package is only learning the mechanics of that software. The underlying skill of knowing how a board should be built is already present, which is why the second board is faster than the first.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just like learning the mechanics of that specific software

claims.claim_text: Layout fluency is perishable. A former full-time designer loses speed and would need days or weeks of daily work to recover it, even though the judgment underneath remains.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a skill that you lose

claims.claim_text: Keeping a hand in is cheaper than recovering the skill later. Reading datasheets and doing occasional small work between projects is enough to hold competence in place through months without a design.
claims.quote_verbatim: it probably keeps my hand in

claims.claim_text: On one professional view the open-source tools, however capable for ordinary work, still lack specific features needed at the high end. The speaker explicitly flags the assessment as based on older knowledge, which is the right caveat for any tool comparison.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's still not a pro-level tool
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The opposing position is a deliberate one: use open-source design tools to support open-source hardware even where they are not the easiest choice for the job, and require collaborators to do the same, accepting the friction as the cost of keeping the project accessible.
claims.quote_verbatim: I really believe in using open source software to support my open source hardware
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: The standard that choice is measured against is unforgiving, because buggy tools are genuinely unacceptable when board design is how you earn a living. Frustration with defects is not preciousness, it is a working constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's nothing worse than buggy tools
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Mechanical CAD choice follows the ecosystem rather than the feature comparison. Whichever package has more use where mechanical work meets board design is the one you are more likely to meet at a client, which outweighs a free licence for many practitioners.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's more likely that they are going to be using SolidWorks than Fusion
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Electrical and mechanical co-design has become part of the board designer's job, which exposes a gap for anyone who has always worked in two dimensions. Being very comfortable at board level does not transfer to three-dimensional modelling, and closing that has to be deliberate.
claims.quote_verbatim: as soon as you go 3D, I've never been as strong at that
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The route into mechanical competence is making bad parts. The first brackets one board designer modelled were not mechanically sound, and building unsound parts is what taught the principles that made later ones good.
claims.quote_verbatim: by building parts that sucked, I learned how to build better parts
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Understanding electromagnetic compatibility improves board design, product design and firmware simultaneously, partly because some compatibility problems turn out to be fixable in firmware once you understand the mechanism.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you understand EMC, you'll definitely be a better PCB and a better product designer

claims.claim_text: Treating board design as a drawing exercise changes which tool is appropriate. A real drawing package makes alignment, whole buses and arbitrary curves easy because that is what it was built for, whereas producing artwork inside an EDA tool is like driving a screw with a knife.
claims.quote_verbatim: screwing in a screw with a knife
claims.speaker: Saar Drimer

claims.claim_text: The design stance behind such a tool can be to refuse a graphical interface entirely, on the argument that graphical interfaces are where good ideas go to die. The tradeoff is a steeper entry in exchange for scriptability and precision.
claims.quote_verbatim: GUI is where good ideas go to die
claims.speaker: Saar Drimer

claims.claim_text: The stated goal for automated board design is a compiler analogy: take the schematic, extract everything that defines what the board must do, and emit a manufacturable board that has been verified against physics and design rules without human routing.
claims.quote_verbatim: our ultimate goal is to start with circuit schematics and then output a ready to go PCB
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: The precedent making that plausible is FPGA place and route, where designers stopped drawing logic by hand once the tool produced a timing report that could be trusted, and where the compute could simply be thrown at a cluster for faster turns.
claims.quote_verbatim: if the timing passes on the report and you know, all the other checks pass, you're good to go

claims.claim_text: The disanalogy is visibility. Board layout is intensely visual in a way that programmable logic place and route is not, which is a real obstacle to accepting a result you cannot inspect the same way.
claims.quote_verbatim: how visual PCB layout is

claims.claim_text: Autorouters are advanced tools for advanced designers rather than a shortcut for beginners. Using one before you can do the job manually removes the feedback that teaches you what a good board looks like.
claims.quote_verbatim: An auto router is a tool, a very advanced tool for advanced PCB designers
claims.episode_title: Autorouter, Datasheets & Obscure Chips - Cloddish Collegiate Conversations

claims.claim_text: A point-and-click board configurator that assembles known modules onto one board has a narrow but real market: someone who needs twenty of something, has no interest in electronics, and does not want to hand-wire twenty assemblies.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't want to hand wire 20 of them

claims.claim_text: Compared against hiring, that service looks expensive: a competent engineer could do the same design in roughly twenty hours. What is actually being sold is avoided activation energy, since finding, briefing and taking the risk on that engineer is itself work.
claims.quote_verbatim: are you going to go and source that person yourself

claims.claim_text: The effort in a real board is routinely underestimated. A genuinely complex product board that has to fit a mechanical envelope can absorb a month of full-time work, and that is competent pace rather than slow.
claims.quote_verbatim: i've i've worked a month on a pcb right and it's not because i'm slow

claims.claim_text: Desktop trace-printing machines are not a press-print path from an existing design. The board has to be redesigned around the machine's limits, components cannot go on the second side, and an existing layout has to be redone entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to redesign your board to fit the technology
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: A plain flexible board is essentially no different to design or order than a rigid one: you specify flex and a thin stack-up instead of standard laminate, and everything else is unchanged. The complexity begins only when flex and rigid layers are combined in one part.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is basically virtually no difference between designing and getting a normal board made and getting a flex board made
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A radio section that has passed certification is reusable capital. Once a design works, leave the antenna section untouched and change sensors and interfaces around it, and the next product has a good chance of passing compliance on the same basis.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you find a working design, you just don't touch the antenna section

claims.claim_text: Antennas have to be considered at the start of a design rather than at the end. Left until last, the antenna gets a poor location with insufficient clearance, and by then nobody will fund the changes that would fix it.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you think about antenna in the beginning you take that into account
claims.speaker: Katerina Galitskaya
claims.episode_title: All About Antennas with Katerina Galitskaya

claims.claim_text: For common 2.4 GHz modules the published guidelines are forgiving enough that a non-specialist can place the antenna correctly by following them. Anything more complex than a standard inverted-F warrants an antenna engineer and simulation.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can place it yourself even if you are not antenna engineer
claims.speaker: Katerina Galitskaya
claims.episode_title: All About Antennas with Katerina Galitskaya

claims.claim_text: Module abstraction is a supply-risk strategy as much as a convenience: standardise on one open module footprint chosen for easy routing at a comfortable 0.8 millimetre pitch, and the processor underneath can change without a redesign of the carrier board or an expensive stack-up.
claims.quote_verbatim: we try to choose a footprint that's easy to route
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: Board design and chip design differ sharply in how much you can trust your components. On silicon there may be a hundred qualified device types that are known to work, whereas a board designer selects among millions of parts and may be using a footprint of entirely unknown provenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can download a footprint that, that Johnny made a few years ago that you have no idea if this footprint is good or not
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Chip and board design are ultimately the same activity of putting shapes on a planar surface, and closer integration between the two toolchains would remove a familiar compromise: adding board layers purely because the pin you need is on the wrong side of the die.
claims.quote_verbatim: the pin you want to use is on the wrong side of the chip

claims.claim_text: For hiring, demonstrated work outweighs credentials. Being able to show boards you designed and built, and to bring the hardware itself to the interview, is what makes the educational background secondary.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can demonstrate that you've laid out your own boards
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: The advice for changing roles is to commit to one substantial project with real money and real months behind it. The object can be pointless; what matters is that the effort is serious enough to function as example work.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would find a project, a meaty project, and make a commitment to it

claims.claim_text: A specific way to approach a design engineer whose job you want: take one of their products apart, obtain the schematic, and ask why they made a particular choice. Design engineers will talk at length about their own designs, which turns an awkward request into a technical conversation.
claims.quote_verbatim: why did you do it this way?

claims.claim_text: A four-year personal project spanning four complete redesigns took one engineer from having done nothing beyond simple through-hole boards to confidently taking a set of requirements through to a working, software-running board with fine-pitch parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: I hadn't even done like assembly of a BGA
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Designing boards and assembling them are separate tasks that appeal to different people, and plenty of excellent designers would never assemble anything themselves. Design also has days that simply do not flow, which one practitioner compares to writer's block.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's almost like writer's block
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: Moving a design between CAD packages means recreating it rather than converting it. One tool migration meant redoing five or six complete boards from scratch, which is the real cost of a tool decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: I went to all the effort to redo the whole design
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A schematic tool that cannot carry you through to a board leaves the hard part undone. Sharing and capturing circuits is comparatively easy; the remaining effort of turning it into a physical board is where the work actually is.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to go that extra 10% and actually design your board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: The better structure for such a tool is interoperation with existing layout packages rather than rebuilding the whole flow in-house. Building it all yourself preserves control at the cost of the thing users actually need.
claims.quote_verbatim: what they should have done is worked with a company that actually makes layout software
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: Two workable panelisation approaches: use a tool that duplicates the boards from a linked source file while you manually draw the rails, fiducials and mounting holes around them, or simply copy the whole board within one file. The linked approach guarantees the copies match.
claims.quote_verbatim: it duplicates the PCBs, but then you manually draw in all the stuff around it

claims.claim_text: Publishing design files in a proprietary format matters less than the argument suggests. Only a small percentage of people ever rebuild a board from source, and for a design of twenty or thirty parts, redrawing it in your own package takes a few hours.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you want to lay it out in your own package, it only takes you a few hours
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: At the precision extreme the board becomes part of the measurement. Voltage reference designs use exotic cutouts so that thermal expansion of the laminate cannot put uneven tension on the package leads, because that stress alone shifts the output by fractions of a part per million.
claims.quote_verbatim: if your board thermally expands a little bit, then that could put uneven tension on the legs of the IC
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A useful way to consume factory and process content is as passive accumulation rather than immediate application: building a mental library of things worth considering next time a similar design comes up.
claims.quote_verbatim: building a mental library of like things that I should be looking into

claims.claim_text: Board design is frequently absent from university curricula altogether, which is why so many engineers meet it first at work or in a hobby project despite it being central to building anything physical.
claims.quote_verbatim: We didn't have even have anything about, you know, PCB design at university
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

attribution_notes: One passage carries no episode number and was dropped as uncitable.
ep515, ep523, ep703, ep250 passages are flagged attribution_reliable:false in the bundle; claims drawn from them carry speaker null.

Several passages label the host as speaker where the words are plainly the interviewee's (ep472 P59, ep626 P86, ep678 P93, ep516); those claims carry speaker null and are content-attributed in the claim text.

Scope note: placement and routing rules, bare-board fabrication economics and schematic capture and review are covered by the sibling pcb-layout, pcb-fabrication and schematic articles; this packet deliberately takes the surrounding process, tooling and role angles.
